# Berge–Fulkerson Conjecture for Bridgeless Cubic Planar Graphs

**Answer: No — the conjecture is not open for bridgeless cubic planar graphs. It is settled (true), as a direct consequence of the Four Color Theorem.**

## Proof

**Definitions.** The Berge–Fulkerson conjecture asserts that every bridgeless cubic graph $G$ admits six perfect matchings $M_1,\dots,M_6$ such that every edge of $G$ belongs to exactly two of them. Equivalently, $G$ has a 2-fold cover by perfect matchings, which is equivalent to the fractional chromatic index $\chi'_f(G)=3$.

**Key equivalence (Tait, 1880).** A cubic graph is 3-edge-colorable if and only if its edge set can be partitioned into three perfect matchings (a 1-factorization). This is immediate: in a proper 3-edge-coloring of a cubic graph, each color class is a 1-factor (a perfect matching), since every vertex is incident to exactly one edge of each color.

**Four Color Theorem ⇒ 3-edge-colorability of bridgeless cubic planar graphs.** By the Four Color Theorem (Appel–Haken, 1976; confirmed by Robertson–Sanders–Seymour–Thomas, 1997), every planar graph is 4-vertex-colorable. Tait showed that 4-vertex-colorability of a bridgeless cubic planar graph is equivalent to 3-edge-colorability of that graph. Concretely, given a proper 4-vertex-coloring with colors $\{0,1,2,3\}$, one assigns to each edge $uv$ the color $\{a \in \mathbb{Z}_2^2 : \text{color}(u)+\text{color}(v) = a\}$ — the three nonzero elements of $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$ give three edge colors, and this is a proper 3-edge-coloring. (The bridgeless condition ensures no edge is a cut-edge, which is necessary for a cubic graph to admit a perfect matching at all, via Petersen's theorem.)

Therefore every bridgeless cubic planar graph is 3-edge-colorable, hence admits a 1-factorization $E = M_1 \sqcup M_2 \sqcup M_3$ into three perfect matchings.

**1-factorization ⇒ Berge–Fulkerson.** Given the 1-factorization $M_1, M_2, M_3$, take the six perfect matchings
$$M_1, M_1, M_2, M_2, M_3, M_3.$$
Every edge lies in exactly one of $M_1, M_2, M_3$, hence in exactly two of the six listed matchings. This is precisely the Berge–Fulkerson configuration. $\square$

**Remark on scope.** The Berge–Fulkerson conjecture remains open in general — the hard cases are bridgeless cubic graphs that are *not* 3-edge-colorable (snarks), such as the Petersen graph. The planar restriction removes all such cases because the Four Color Theorem forces 3-edge-colorability. Thus the conjecture is trivially true on the planar subclass and the open problem lives entirely among non-planar (and necessarily non-3-edge-colorable) cubic graphs.

### PROOF COMPLETE
